§ 02 · Interconnection

Three distinct paths
to the grid.

Most Oregon solar sites are constrained to a single interconnection approach. This site offers three — at different scales, through different utilities, with different developer profiles. All three are independently verified through public utility data sources.

Path 01 · Distribution

PGE Barnes Substation

10–30 MW · 477 ft from property

Barnes is a 13 kV PGE distribution substation. PGE's published Distribution Resource Plan data shows two transformers at 21.2 MVA each. The closest feeder, Barnes-Boone, has 0.1 MW of distributed generation connected, zero in queue, and is not generation-limited.

Initial third-party review (Scout Land Consultants, May 2026) correctly flagged that Barnes is too small for utility-scale BESS. The open feeder hosting capacity makes it well-suited for distribution-tier projects that don't need transmission-level interconnection.

Path 02 · PGE Transmission

115 kV → Bethel

50–100+ MW · On-property

A PGE 115 kV transmission line runs along Turner Road through the property and terminates at PGE Bethel Substation — one of PGE's major 115/230 kV transmission switching nodes in the central Willamette Valley. Verified via Oregon DOE Geohub Electric Transmission Lines dataset.

Bethel is referenced extensively in PGE's 2024-2025 Local Transmission Plan as a key transmission node receiving capacity upgrades. Direct 115 kV access to Bethel means access to PGE's full transmission backbone — and PGE as the off-take utility, separate from PacifiCorp territory.

§ 04 · Floodplain & Hydraulic

Floodplain
is a feature.

Most Oregon solar projects fight EFU farmland restrictions. This site has the inverse problem — it's industrial-zoned (good) but has Mill Creek floodplain across the central section. For traditional industrial development, that's a constraint. For elevated agrivoltaic solar, it's the most valuable acreage on the site.

Solar is permitted in floodplain

Under federal NFIP, Oregon DLCD guidance, and Salem's Ordinance No. 6-25 (effective July 9, 2025), ground-mounted solar is permitted in Special Flood Hazard Areas subject to floodplain development standards. The post-2024 NFIP-ESA framework requires no net loss in three proxies for natural floodplain function:

  • Flood storage (don't displace volume the floodplain absorbs)
  • Water quality (manage stormwater to standard)
  • Vegetated habitat (preserve or enhance riparian function)

Elevated agrivoltaic solar satisfies all three by design. Panels mounted 8-12 ft above grade preserve flood conveyance. Native vegetation underneath improves water quality and provides pollinator-friendly habitat. No fill required for the array itself.

Reframe: Acreage historically classified as "unusable" under traditional industrial assumptions becomes the most valuable acreage under an elevated-racking solar configuration. The floodplain is the asset.

WEST Consultants hydraulic analysis

A 2D HEC-RAS unsteady hydraulic evaluation has been completed for the site by WEST Consultants, Inc. of Salem (the same firm that authored the City of Salem Stormwater Masterplan and the Mill Creek Basin Flood Risk Reduction Study). Contracted through Westech Engineering, the project civil engineer of record.

  • Erik McCarthy, PE, CFM — author
  • Hans Hadley, PE, CFM, VP — reviewer
  • 2.2-mile model extent · calibrated to ±0.00 ft on 2012 flood
  • FEMA-grade methodology · 100-yr base flood at 9,540 cfs

The analysis demonstrates zero net upstream BFE impact (-0.01 ft average) and no impact downstream at the Turner Road bridge. On-property impacts are subject to optimization based on final development scenario.

Value to a buyer: A calibrated HEC-RAS model of Mill Creek represents 6-12 months and $100K+ of work. A solar developer's hydraulic engineer can re-run scenarios on this model in weeks, not start from scratch in months.
§ 05 · Value Optimization

Stackable
incentives.

Three potentially stackable incentive layers that a sophisticated developer can pursue on this site. Each one is real but each requires buyer-side verification — none are baked into the asking price. Listed honestly so they're not surprises.

Layer 01 · State

Oregon SIP Tax Abatement

Marion County participates in Oregon's Strategic Investment Program. Capital investments above the SIP threshold qualify for 15-year property tax abatement on improvements.

For a 100 MW solar project, NPV impact in the $5-15M range. For a hybrid solar + data center, materially higher.

Verification: Marion County Economic Development confirmation that the IC/IG parcel is within the SIP-eligible boundary; SIP application process runs through the county and state.

Layer 02 · Federal

IRA ITC Adders

Base 30% solar ITC, with potential adders for: Energy Community (+10%, fossil fuel employment census-tract qualification), Domestic Content (+10%), and Prevailing Wage + Apprenticeship (+10% if not paid at scale).

Stacked maximum can reach 50%+ ITC on a qualifying project.

Verification: Census-tract analysis for Energy Community designation. Domestic Content and Prevailing Wage are buyer-controlled procurement and labor decisions.

Layer 03 · Local

Mill Creek URA Extension

The Salem Mill Creek Industrial URA covers 650 acres adjacent to this site and provides TIF financing for infrastructure (roads, utilities, traffic). Project-specific infrastructure (Mill Creek bridge, Turner Rd improvements, water booster pump) totals ~$20-30M in current cost estimates.

URA boundary extension or a new adjacent URA designation could provide TIF financing for portions of that infrastructure scope, reducing developer carry.

Verification: Conversation with City of Salem Urban Renewal Agency. Requires City Council action; political work, not free.

§ 06 · Open Questions

The open
questions.

We've spent four years getting this site ready. We've verified the interconnection paths, modeled the hydraulics, walked the entitlement process, and assembled the engineering team. What we haven't done is build solar in Oregon. If you have, these are the questions we'd genuinely value your read on. The deal room is open. Owner-direct.

01

Sequencing the two transmission paths.

Three interconnection paths through two utilities: PGE 115 kV to Bethel, PacifiCorp 230 kV on-property, PGE Barnes 13 kV at the boundary. Pursue both PGE and PacifiCorp transmission queues in parallel? Pick one and commit? The answer probably depends on the developer's existing utility relationships and queue positions. We'd value your view on how a serious developer evaluates this kind of dual-utility site.

02

The community solar carve-out question.

Barnes-Boone feeder shows 0.1 MW connected and 1.99% saturation. A 3 MW Oregon CSP project sits comfortably under the cap, with stackable additional projects possible. Is the carve-out worth pursuing alongside utility-scale, or does it dilute capital and attention from the larger play? We've heard arguments both ways and don't have strong conviction.

03

Agrivoltaic foundations in regulated floodway.

Salem Ord. 6-25 (effective July 2025) requires no-net-loss across flood storage, water quality, and vegetated habitat. Elevated racking 8-12 ft above grade satisfies all three by design. What's your preferred foundation system for an elevated array in Zone AE soils with elevated water table — helical piles, ballasted, or driven post? The geotech is in progress; this would be useful input as we structure the diligence package.

04

PacifiCorp 2025 OR Small-Scale RFP timing.

Pricing held firm through June 30, 2026. COD by December 31, 2029. Is this site competitive in that window, or is the queue work too long to hit the COD requirement? A developer evaluating this site in the next 60 days might bid into that window; a developer evaluating in 6 months probably can't. Worth your read.

05

Bethel topology and SIS implications.

The PGE 115 kV line on Turner Rd terminates at Bethel — a major 115/230 kV transmission node with multiple lines converging. Bethel is referenced in PGE's 2024-2025 Local Transmission Plan as receiving capacity upgrades. Does the Bethel topology change the System Impact Study calculus relative to a radial-line interconnect? We're not transmission engineers; you may be.
